contract_plain_english: For a constant real matrix A and a differentiable vector state q, define the linear flux by f(q) = A q. Then the conservation-law derivative partial_x(f(q)) is A q_x, so the conservation law is exactly the constant-coefficient linear system q_t + A q_x = 0.

binders: A state q(x,t) with values in R^m.
A constant real matrix A of size m by m.
A flux f: R^m -> R^m defined by f(v) = A v.
conclusions: The constant-coefficient linear system q_t + A q_x = 0 is exactly the conservation law q_t + partial_x(f(q)) = 0 with linear flux f(q) = A q.
definitions_and_conventions: A q is ordinary real matrix-vector multiplication.
A linear flux has no additive constant term and maps R^m to R^m.
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives.
Constancy of A permits the identity partial_x(A q) = A q_x.
hypotheses: A is independent of x, t, and q.
q is spatially differentiable so that partial_x(A q) = A q_x.
implicit_context: The problem is a one-dimensional homogeneous first-order system.
The conservation-law specialization is algebraic and separate from whether A satisfies the spectral conditions for hyperbolicity.
The scalar case is included when m = 1.

details: Substituting f(q) = A q into q_t + partial_x(f(q)) = 0 produces q_t + A q_x = 0 because A is constant.
The two displayed forms describe the same PDE under the stated differentiability.
q has m real components and A is an m by m real matrix, so both A q and A q_x are vectors in R^m.
No eigenvalue or eigenvector hypothesis is used in the flux substitution itself.
Such spectral conditions matter only if the system is additionally claimed to be hyperbolic.

undebatable_constraints: The flux is exactly f(q) = A q.
A is a constant real m by m matrix.
The state and flux have the same dimension m.
The conservation derivative is partial_x(A q) = A q_x, relying on constancy of A.
The resulting equation retains the plus sign and zero right-hand side: q_t + A q_x = 0.
The algebraic specialization does not by itself impose hyperbolicity spectral conditions.
